documents.abstract: Introduction: Hotel housekeepers sustain the core functioning of the hospitality industry yet perform demanding, repetitive, and undervalued work associated with substantial physical and psychosocial risks. Understanding how working conditions shape health, motivation, and lived experience is essential for informing prevention strategies and promoting decent work. Methods A sequential narrative review and qualitative meta -synthesis were conducted to integrate and reinterpret evidence across disciplines and study designs. Searches covered five academic databases and gray literature without year or language limits. Studies were screened using predefined criteria, appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, and synthesized through narrative, tabular, and meta -analytical thematic analysis, with findings interpreted through the JD-R framework. Results Findings revealed employment precarity, work intensification, musculoskeletal pain, chemical and biological hazards, and elevated stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Time pressure fostered coping strategies such as skipping meals and delaying bathroom use. Gendered labor divisions, discrimination, and negative supervision contributed to invisibility and limited autonomy. Workers also expressed pride, intrinsic motivation, and collective action to make their contributions visible. Conclusions This review demonstrates that housekeeping is characterized by structural precarity and cumulative health burdens alongside resilience and emerging activism. Improving occupational health requires organizational and policy transformations: realistic workloads, safer equipment, secure contracts, participatory risk management, and leadership practices grounded in dignity and fairness; rather than reliance on individual coping. Structural change is essential to advance safer, more equitable, and sustainable workplaces in the hospitality sector. The JD-R framework highlights the need to reduce demand and strengthen resources.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Biodiversity informatics has made occurrence records widely accessible, yet many databases remain optimized for human browsing rather than structured machine consumption by large language models (LLMs) and AI agents. This creates a bottleneck: analytical capacity is accelerating while biodiversity evidence remains fragmented, weakly documented, and difficult to cite reproducibly. Here we introduce evidence manifestation, a design approach that transforms raw occurrence data into versioned, citable, machine-readable knowledge artifacts with explicit provenance. Using World of Crayfish®, we implement this concept through Species Exposure Bundles (SEBs) that package curated occurrence snapshots, spatial layers, derived range metrics (extent of occurrence, area of occupancy), geographic summaries (basins, administrative units, protected areas), and machine-readable metadata exposed via stable identifiers (JSON/GeoJSON). To validate real-world utility, we conducted controlled LLM query tests contrasting closed-book baseline (T0), web search (T1), and manifest-directed retrieval with SEB access (T2) across four AI applications. Nine endemic crayfish species with minimal online documentation were compared against one high web-visibility control species (Procambarus virginalis). For endemic taxa, closed-book performance was low (mean 1.78/8; 47% complete failures), web search improved but remained variable (mean 4.22/8; 19% failures), and manifest-directed retrieval produced consistently high performance (mean 6.97/8; 0% failures; 50.0% perfect scores). The control species achieved 5.75/8 under closed-book conditions (T0), exceeding endemic web-search performance and approaching endemic manifest-directed performance, highlighting accessibility gaps for underrepresented taxa. These results position evidence manifestation as a practical, reproducible infrastructure pattern for AI-assisted biodiversity synthesis and conservation workflows.

Abstract This paper argues that the operational value of machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) cannot be assessed through verification skill alone. Instead, acceptance depends on support for the core functions of operational meteorology: understanding, translating and communicating. Current MLWP systems show strong performance but lack the interpretability, diagnostic depth and stability required for trust in safety‐critical contexts. The paper highlights the need for closer collaboration between developers and operational users and identifies a key future role for artificial intelligence (AI) in supporting data triage and human decision‐making.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is disrupting creative work and challenging occupational identities, yet limited research has examined how creators experience and respond to these changes. Drawing on Albert Ellis’s ABC model, this study investigates relationships among GenAI adoption, identity threat, job crafting, and identity consequences. Using a two-stage exploratory mixed-method design with digital content creators in China, we combined BERTopic analysis of 2994 open-ended responses with structural equation modelling of matched survey data from 1698 creators. The findings show that GenAI is widely perceived through coexisting beliefs about threat, opportunity, and the unknown, and that these beliefs give rise to differentiated job crafting behaviours, including approach crafting, avoidance crafting, and identity crafting. Notably, identity crafting plays an important role in fostering a responsible creative identity and self-actualization. This study advances theorizing on AI technological innovation and creative labour by showing how job crafting translates GenAI disruption into responsibility-oriented and meaning-centered identity reshaping. It also offers actionable insights for creators, platforms, and creative communities seeking to support collaborative, sustainable, and ethically grounded human–AI co-creation.

Steering an LLM agent means deciding whether to correct it, at which step, and with which mechanism. Uncertainty is often used to decide when to correct an agent, but whether it can guide these decisions remains unclear. We steer agent trajectories separately at every non-terminal step with each of four mechanisms and run each continuation to completion. The resulting stepwise outcome table (SOT) holds about 82,000 counterfactual continuations of 1,864 trajectories from three benchmarks and two agents. It shows that uncertainty can identify failing trajectories, but that no single signal reliably locates the step at which steering helps. We therefore propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor, offline or online, that learns from SOT the value of steering at each step and decides where to steer by it. A harm-budgeted trigger decides whether to steer, limiting the fraction of successful trajectories that VoS disturbs. VoS improves on unmodified execution in all 12 settings of benchmark, agent, and offline or online use, by 7.8 points on average, and outperforms the strongest of five existing uncertainty-triggered methods in 11, by 2.9 points on average. Ablations show that training on measured outcomes and a tight harm budget are both essential.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Voluntary use of AI-supported learning platforms may differ across features, while aggregate logs cannot show whether teachers act on analytics. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate AI Sensei’s architecture, logged activity across platform features, self-reported feature use and student feedback. METHODS: An observational pilot analysed logs for 205 students and an anonymous questionnaire (N = 100). Training quizzes and feedback were programmed; chat used generative AI. RESULTS: All 205 students submitted training quizzes and self-check tests (1,999 and 481 submissions, respectively); 164 (80.0%) sent at least one chat message. In the separate anonymous questionnaire, 91% selected quizzes/tests and 17% the chat assistant; 94% agreed that combining teacher support with AI Sensei was more beneficial than teaching without the platform. CONCLUSION: Structured practice merits refinement; teacher-facing analytics require evaluation for actionability.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) are usually frozen after deployment, so they do not learn from the cases they solve. This is especially concerning in medicine, where new clinical evidence, updated guidelines, and new therapies can change established practice. Fine-tuning can update the model, but it requires access to model weights and additional training. Parameter-free methods avoid training, but they may overfit a fixed validation set, lack reliable domain knowledge, or lose visual details by saving experience only as text. To address these limitations, we present a model-agnostic framework that allows frozen LLMs and VLMs to learn from deployment experience through three forms of external expertise: a Skill that guides reasoning and tool use, a Knowledge Memory that stores reliable facts supported by earlier cases or trusted external evidence, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base that keeps visual examples and guides the model to relate each retrieved case to the current image. Instead of relying on a fixed validation set, a validation strategy keeps an update only if it helps on new cases without degrading performance on earlier ones. Across six benchmarks covering clinical diagnosis, clinical workflows, medical reasoning, and medical and non-medical visual reasoning, and with four open-weight and closed-source base models, our framework improves performance during online deployment by up to 34.2% over the base model on medical tasks, generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without further optimization, and works in non-medical domains.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: A limited claim about the relation between transformer language models and Husserl's account of time-consciousness, read through Jeff Yoshimi's chapter "What do LLMs tell us about phenomenology?" (forthcoming, Routledge) and his 2016 formalization of Husserl. The note argues that the context-window analogy is weaker than it looks, that the transformer has two temporal regimes (a closed and a growing sequence) rather than one, and that its weights are the residue of a training process that formally resembles Yoshimi's learning rule λ. In a frozen session nothing passes from the window to the weights: there is updating without sedimentation. Asked whether the resemblance is more than formal, Yoshimi judged formal resemblance the safer reading; his answer is paraphrased in §4. Three sentences from correspondence are quoted with permission. The note does not claim that language models are conscious.

Uncertainty permeates healthcare due to the intrinsic variability of biological processes, the ambiguity of clinical observations, and the incompleteness of medical data. Conventional artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning methods frequently fall short in such environments because they typically assume precise, abundant, and homogeneous datasets that rarely exist in clinical practice. Fuzzy set theory, grounded in graded membership and partial truth, offers a mathematically robust basis for representing vagueness, while fuzzy logic provides a reasoning mechanism capable of drawing reliable inferences under imprecise, inconsistent, or linguistically formulated conditions. Together, these approaches have facilitated the development of hybrid fuzzy–AI systems that support human-aligned reasoning, enhance interpretability, and strengthen decision reliability across data-scarce healthcare settings. A growing body of work demonstrates the value of fuzzy methodologies in diagnostic decision support, treatment planning, risk stratification, and healthcare operations. Advancements include type-1, type-2, intuitionistic, and hesitant fuzzy sets, as well as neuro-fuzzy models, fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making, and fuzzy–deep learning architectures. Ongoing challenges persist regarding data heterogeneity, interpretability, and clinical validation, while emerging research directions point toward explainable fuzzy–AI systems, connected health monitoring, and uncertainty-aware digital twins.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Gene expression is widely measured in biomedicine, yet clinical outcome prediction remains challenging due to high dimensionality, strong feature correlations, and limited labeled data. Large self-supervised transcriptomic foundation models often fail to outperform simple supervised baselines. Tabular foundation models offer an alternative through in-context learning, but are typically pretrained on generic synthetic data rather than transcriptomic structure. We ask whether transcriptomics-aware pretraining, rather than scale, is the missing ingredient. Towards this end, we introduce GeneICL, a 4.2M-parameter tabular foundation model combining a semi-synthetic pretraining prior built from measured bulk expression profiles with a parameter-efficient recurrent architecture. We further enable right-censored survival prediction via a training-free reduction to regression using Cox partial-likelihood residuals. We evaluate GeneICL on 80 clinical outcome-prediction tasks spanning classification, regression, and survival. Tabular foundation models consistently outperform self-supervised transcriptomic models, while GeneICL achieves the best overall rank among evaluated foundation models and tuned baselines. GeneICL does so with up to 387$\times$ fewer parameters, no gradient updates at inference, and predictions within seconds on a laptop CPU.

Background Generative artificial intelligence is progressively reshaping study-travel—a curriculum-embedded educational practice. Yet, the psychological processes governing upper-primary and middle-school students’ adoption of such technology in this context remain underexplored. Prior technology acceptance inquiries have predominantly centered on adult populations, leaving adolescent cognitive-developmental contingencies unaddressed. Objective This investigation aimed to elucidate the differential roles of affective versus utilitarian drivers in shaping study-travel participants’ anticipated intentions to adopt GenAI, and to determine whether these pathways differ by grade level. Method We constructed an integrative model grounded in the extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2), supplemented by Piaget’s developmental framework. The model incorporated perceived enjoyment as a mediator and perceived risk as a direct negative antecedent, with grade level specified as a moderator of selected pathways. Survey data from 741 students in grades 4–9, drawn from twelve schools across six Chinese cities, were analyzed using structural equation modeling, multi-group comparisons, and cluster-robust standard errors to account for the nested sampling structure. Measurement invariance across grade groups was established prior to structural comparisons. Results Perceived enjoyment emerged as the largest estimated predictor of adoption intention in this sample ( β = 0.43, p < 0.001), surpassing performance expectancy ( β = 0.30, p < 0.001). Enjoyment fully mediated social influence effects and partially transmitted performance expectancy‘s influence. Perceived risk exerted a significant suppressive effect ( β = −0.24, p < 0.001), with primary students exhibiting approximately twice the inhibitory magnitude of middle-school counterparts. Grade significantly moderated the performance expectancy–intention relationship, and provided borderline evidence for moderation of the risk–intention relationship, indicating systematic grade-related differences in how these pathways operate. Conclusion These findings advance technology acceptance theory by introducing grade-related contingency and establishing an “affective–efficacy” dual-channel model. Practical implications for designing grade-differentiated educational AI products are discussed.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly influencing how students write, create, reflect, solve problems, and engage with learning in higher education. However, the evidence remains divided, particularly regarding motivation, engagement, creativity, perception, self-regulation, and psychologically informed learning design. This study presents a PRISMA-ScR-based scoping review of GenAI in higher education from a motivational and psychological perspective. The final corpus included 195 studies published between 2023 and 2025 within a specified eligibility window of January 2021 to December 2025. Records were dual screened, coded using a structured framework, and analyzed across psychological focus, thematic constructs, GenAI tools, study designs, outcomes, contextual characteristics, self-determination theory (SDT) needs, equity, and evidence strength. The screening agreement was 81.9%, with Cohen’s κ = 0.642. Motivation was the most common primary focus (31.3%), followed by perception (26.7%), engagement (18.5%), creativity (15.4%), and general/other (8.2%). The literature was dominated by ChatGPT and general GenAI systems, while survey-based and observational evidence was far more common than experimental evidence, longitudinal research, or studies reporting objective performance outcomes. Among 155 empirical studies, mixed or conditional outcomes were most frequent (46.5%), compared with predominantly positive findings (21.9%). SDT related evidence was most common for competence (42.6%), followed by autonomy (29.7%) and relatedness (22.6%), although direct measurement was rare. Based on these findings, the study proposes the GenAI engagement framework, a literature informed structure that organizes five recurring components of GenAI supported learning without assuming a fixed sequence or causal pathway. The framework is not presented as a validated causal model, but as a structured basis for future research and instructional design. The findings suggest that the educational value of GenAI depends less on the technology itself than on how it is guided, evaluated, and integrated into meaningful learning activities.

documents.abstract: Emergency messaging such as extreme-weather reports and earthquake instructions can involve high stakes, to the extent that translation errors can lead to tragic consequences. The use of machine translation or generative artificial intelligence might therefore not be recommended. On the other hand, time savings in the initial translation can allow greater investments of resources in revision and authorization processes, as well as a wider range of target languages. An experiment with generative AI translations of an earthquake instruction text from English into Chinese and Spanish shows that use of discourse-specific prompts can considerably improve understandability and actionability, although the translations may still not be trusted by translators. Human revision is still required, not only to detect errors but also because of the ethical need for someone to take responsibility for any errors or delays in such messaging.

Introduction Generative AI is increasingly used to support learning in higher education, yet the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and students’ perceived academic performance, as well as the conditions under which this association varies, remains unclear. Drawing on social cognitive theory and AI literacy research, this study tested whether generative AI-assisted learning use was indirectly associated with perceived academic performance through self-efficacy and whether AI literacy conditioned the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy. Methods Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 376 undergraduates at universities in China. An item-level latent interaction structural equation was estimated using a matched-pair product-indicator approach. Results The model showed positive associations between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy ( β = 0.207, p < 0.001) and between self-efficacy and perceived academic performance ( β = 0.199, p < 0.001). The latent interaction between generative AI-assisted learning use and AI literacy was positive ( B = 0.068, 95% bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval [0.012, 0.123]), indicating that the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy was stronger at higher levels of AI literacy. The conditional indirect association was not statistically significant at low AI literacy but was positive and statistically significant at the mean and high levels. The index of moderated mediation was 0.011 (95% bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval [0.002, 0.026]), indicating that the indirect association varied across levels of AI literacy. Discussion These findings describe a theory-consistent conditional pattern of cross-sectional associations but do not establish temporal or causal ordering.

documents.abstract: Accurate hierarchical multi-label classification of construction accident narratives is vital, yet traditional methods struggle with the Occupational Injury and Illness Classification System (OIICS), which contains over 2000 labels across four attributes with four-level hierarchies and is subject to taxonomic updates. This paper proposes the Adaptive Generative Construction Classification (AGCC), a taxonomy-informed generative framework that reformulates coding as structured sequence-to-sequence generation. Each attribute is predicted at a variable depth using leaf codes, while taxonomy-informed serialization and semantic-aware label verbalization promote hierarchical consistency. AGCC incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. On OIICS 3.0, AGCC achieves 74.36% Weighted-F1 (Flat) and 84.66% Weighted-F1 (Hierarchical), outperforming full fine-tuning of FLAN-T5-Large by 4.41 and 2.74 percentage points, respectively. Macro-F1 improves by 5.78 and 5.53 percentage points, respectively, while 3.2% of parameters are trainable. AGCC transfers across backbones and demonstrates robustness to taxonomy shifts, offering an accurate and scalable solution for construction safety coding under evolving taxonomies.

Geospatial information is used in education as disciplinary content and as a learning technology, while computational geospatial research increasingly employs artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and remote sensing. This study maps the publication performance and thematic structure of a broad Scopus corpus at the interface of geospatial technology and education from 2002 to 2025. A PRISMA-guided review and bibliometric analysis were conducted on 125 documents from 68 sources using bibliometrix and Biblioshiny in R. The corpus showed an annual publication growth rate of 10.99%, an average of 11.93 citations per document, and 2.81 authors per document. The Journal of Geography was the most productive source, while De Lázaro-Torres and De Miguel González were the most productive authors. Co-word analysis identified an educational GIS cluster, a geospatial technology and learning cluster, and a computational geospatial cluster containing GeoAI-related terms. The increased visibility of the computational cluster in 2022–2025 indicates an emerging thematic orientation, not evidence that GeoAI has replaced GIS-based education or already dominates educational practice. Because the search expression included the broad term learning and the corpus retained several technical geospatial records, the findings should be interpreted as an exploratory map of the education–technology interface. The proposed instructional sequence is therefore a theory-informed research proposition that requires empirical validation

It addresses: AI-assisted governance Algorithmic decision systems State observation and estimation Uncertainty representation Feedback and control architectures Cybernetic governance Human oversight Human intervention Escalation procedures Human override Decision support versus autonomous action Safety constraints Verification and validation Adversarial testing Bias assessment Disparate-impact assessment Data governance Model integrity Cybersecurity Provenance Auditability Reproducibility High-impact automated decision safeguards Appeal Correction Review Model monitoring Change management Failure containment Computational systems remain subject to applicable law, institutional competence, human-rights safeguards, safety requirements, accountability, oversight, and review. GCED-26 does not treat algorithmic outputs as intrinsically authoritative. Automated recommendations, classifications, predictions, or control signals require appropriate governance arrangements and, where applicable, human review and legally authorized decision pathways. Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine transportation are fundamental to modern human life, but vehicle collisions with wildlife inadvertently kill hundreds of millions of animals across 2000 vertebrate and invertebrate species annually; however, a comprehensive framework to assess and mitigate these mortalities is missing. We identified and compared the most up-to-date information regarding the impacts of transportation on wildlife mortality to determine cross-cutting solutions to this challenging problem. For example, numerous strategies, such as under- or overpasses traversing roads and railways that increase wildlife-habitat connectivity, policies that enforce reduced speed in areas with active wildlife, and passive sensors that detect wildlife to alert nearby ships and vehicles and enable mandatory speed reductions, can reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions. We explored emerging technological advances that could help further reduce future wildlife-vehicle conflicts and provide a path forward for transportation systems. Specifically, we described how the combination of citizen science, artificial intelligence, targeted studies on wildlife demographic impacts, and cost-effective mitigation efforts will be powerful tools to inform needed future policies to decrease ship speed in areas with threatened whale species and reduce rates of wildlife mortality across ecosystems in a fast-moving world.

Advances in sensing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) are moving smart cities toward a Fully Sensed Society (FSS), in which human behavior and states can be continuously inferred. This paper presents the Fully Monitored Public Space (FMPS) as a scaled-down model of the FSS and a smart-city testbed, and examines two questions. First, to what extent can unauthorized external AI outputs be structurally deterred? The previously proposed Verifiable Record of AI Output (VRAIO) binds outputs to Rules, an independent Recorder, tamper-resistant records, audits, and sanctions, making deviations verifiable and attributable. The Recorder, however, checks only the consistency of declared metadata with the Rules, not the output content; false declarations are deterred because unannounced audits and sanctions make their expected benefit smaller than the expected loss upon detection. Second, if such trustworthiness is secured, does it lead to social acceptance of being continuously known by AI? We propose a staged and reversible evaluation framework for the FMPS that distinguishes acceptance grounded in the experience of “no actual harm” and of “benefits” (personal and social) from resignation accompanied by chilling effects. This paper does not answer the question; it presents a method for asking it empirically.

documents.abstract: On-policy distillation post-trains large language model agents by supplying dense, step-level guidance from a teacher policy when the reinforcement-learning reward is sparse and arrives only once per trajectory. Existing instantiations allocate this guidance by the size of the teacher-student divergence at each step, on the single-turn intuition that a large disagreement marks a mistake worth correcting. Once decisions chain over many turns, that rule misfires, since an early drift enters every later context both policies condition on, leaving the teacher consistent with the drifted trajectory instead of flagging its cause, while interchangeable steps register large but outcome-irrelevant divergences. We demonstrate this on an agentic benchmark, where distilling the highest-divergence steps brings no consistent benefit over random selection. To this end, we introduce GraphOPD, the first method to bring graph-based structural augmentation into on-policy distillation for agent capabilities. It reads which steps enabled which later ones from the environment's own record of state changes, immune to the drift that corrupts the teacher-student gap, organizes them into a dependency graph, scores each step by a random-walk stationary distribution over it, and fuses that structural credit with the divergence signal into a trajectory-relative mask concentrating supervision on each rollout's highest-aptitude steps. Across three model scales and eleven baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, GraphOPD shows competitive performance throughout, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +5.8 pp. An executed-replay audit further shows that this structural credit score tracks true causal impact far above chance, that both fused signals are independently necessary, and that the same signal transfers to out-of-domain tool-integrated reasoning.

We present a claim–computation binding audit: a deterministic instrument that verifies whether each claim in an AI-generated analysis is bound to the executed tool call that produced its statistic, classifying each binding (errored / variable-mismatch / stat-mismatch / clean), together with the keyed ground-truth benchmark and the pre-registered, provenance-stamped run corpora on which we ablate it. The setting is agentic statistical root-cause analysis (the Analyze phase of Six Sigma DMAIC), where the trust signals practitioners rely on prove gameable: a no-LLM fill-in-the-blanks template scores 0.867 on a completeness rubric with verified-recall 0, so "complete and well-cited" measures form, not correctness. Applying the audit to a pre-hardening corpus of agentic DMAIC runs (n=23 supported claims, 3 small open-weight models), 52.2% of supported claims (12/23) carry a binding defect even though audit-ID provenance resolves 100%; 6/23 (~26%) are the motivating subclass, a claim citing a real, audit-logged statistic that actually concerns different variables. We call such provenance spoofable. In a pre-registered ablation (180 runs; 45 pairs per contrast; hash-frozen scoring and binding code), the full 12-safeguard stack (base-6 artifact-hygiene checks plus our six correctness safeguards D1–D6, anchored by the claim–computation binding check D1) cuts the run-level binding-defect rate from 28.9% to 2.2% (Holm-corrected p=0.0055). The contrasts isolating single components are not significant (D1–D5: directionally consistent, Holm-corrected p=0.1406; D6: uninformative, 1/45 vs 0/45), so the confirmed effect is stack-level. Descriptively, 9 of the 13 unguarded defective runs are MISSING-only, a class an artifact-existence check can already catch, while the semantic classes (wrong variables, mismatched statistics, or unverifiable statistics; this paper's motivating phenomenon) fall from 4/45 to 0/45 under the full stack. The design was not power-analyzed, and discovery shows no detectable improvement (95% CI on the paired difference spans zero): the safeguards reduce fabricated support, not analytical error. Defects are rarer at larger scale (1/15 unguarded runs at each of a 32B and a frontier-family model, both exploratory) but do not vanish, and binding cleanliness holds on a sealed held-out pair. We contribute a measurement that separates grounded from correct, a detector for spoofable provenance, an honestly-bounded safeguard, and an artifact bundle containing the pre-registration with hash-frozen analysis code, per-run score and binding tables for all five corpora, and per-run summaries (provenance-stamped for the four pre-registered corpora).

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) equipped with terminal access have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating software engineering tasks. However, existing agents remain brittle on long-horizon workflows, where they must repeatedly reconstruct program state scattered across source files, configurations, tests, dependencies, and runtime behavior, leading to increasingly long interaction histories, context explosion, and semantic drift. Large repositories further complicate the identification of task-relevant components. To address these challenges, we introduce \textbf{Dev-Primitives} (\emph{Development Primitives}), a modular and executable abstraction that transforms repository components from passive software artifacts into active participants in software engineering. Each Dev-Primitive pairs a repository artifact with a resident LLM, which gives the artifact an agent-native interface grounded in its own implementation and dependencies, enabling natural-language reasoning, inter-component communication, and localized self-modification. Building on Dev-Primitives, we propose \textbf{HERMES}, a Harness Engineering framework for software engineeRing via Modular Executable Dev-PrimitiveS, which instantiates these primitives at repository scale through a dependency-aware dynamic activation mechanism and a bug diagnosis mechanism that maps execution evidence back to the components that must be revised. Extensive experiments on four software engineering benchmarks demonstrate that HERMES outperforms matched baseline harnesses by 12.4\% on average. Moreover, when paired with strong activation and diagnosis models, HERMES, even with Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives, remains within 4.5\% of the homogeneous GPT-5.6 Sol configuration across all four benchmarks, while reducing inference cost by 26.2\% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, highlighting the importance of harness design in software engineering agents.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the important catalysts to change the practice of healthcare through availability for better patient care, greater efficiency in clinical workflow, and progress in medical research. This chapter will investigate the transformative role of healthcare AI by evaluating its application of diagnostics, therapeutic planning, patient monitoring, personalized medicine, and hospital management systems. There will be further discussion concerning machine learning, natural language processing, and predictive analytics wherein the result will be better decision-making, fewer errors, and an increase in operational efficiency. In addition to this, there will be discussion concerning challenges that are faced, such as privacy issues, ethical issues, and integration with preexisting healthcare infrastructure and the implications that the future of AI-based solutions indicates. This work will synthesize contemporary trends in healthcare, case studies, and the technological applications that have been evolved to explore the important part that AI will have as it continues to develop in creating a more efficient, accurate, and patient-centered system of healthcare delivery.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Tool-augmented speech assistants typically serialize automatic speech recognition, large language model inference, and external tool execution. As a result, tool latency is incurred only after the user has finished speaking and the LLM has identified the required tool calls. We present speculative tool execution for on-device cascaded voice agents, which predicts tool requests from partial ASR hypotheses and initiates tool execution while speech is still being received, thereby reducing end-to-end response latency. Our approach introduces a Predictor module that anticipates tool calls during speech recognition, executes them speculatively, and caches the results. The cached outputs are then injected into the LLM prompt, enabling faster responses. Additionally, to mitigate errors caused by user self-corrections during speech, we employ a rule-based validation mechanism that selectively injects only valid cached results. As a final safeguard, the LLM retains the ability to issue tool calls directly, ensuring that the latency of our framework is upper-bounded by the baseline serial execution pipeline in the worst case. We evaluate our method using live measurements from a fully implemented Android voice assistant. Our approach reduces the median time-to-first-audio from 5.79,s to 4.60,s and decreases the standard deviation from 3.49,s to 2.81,s, resulting in more predictable response latency.

As human--AI interactions become more conversational, full-duplex speech language models capable of natural real-time dialogue are growing in importance. Beyond generating appropriate responses, these models must coordinate turn-taking, backchanneling, and floor management in real time. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a way to refine these behaviors through direct feedback on interaction outcomes. However, existing RL methods either apply timing feedback to a token policy or optimize semantic content, leaving the joint improvement of timing and content unresolved. We introduce HiPLEX, an RL framework that factorizes a pretrained full-duplex text policy into a control policy that decides when to emit content and a conditional content policy that decides what to emit. The first factor selects among 'pad', 'epad', and 'con'. The second selects a token only when 'con' is chosen. This hierarchy describes conditional actions within each frame and uses the model's existing text head. We route timing advantages to the token-group factor through event-causal masks derived from generated speech episodes, and route an LLM-judge semantic advantage to the conditional content factor. Across three Moshi seeds on Full-Duplex-Bench v1, HiPLEX reduces takeover rates during natural user pauses and backchannel opportunities, and shortens post-interruption response latency relative to GRPO, while maintaining comparable judged interruption-response quality. On Moshi and PersonaPlex, HiPLEX better matches pooled human turn-timing and backchannel-rate marginals than GRPO.

Each of the preceding chapters in this book has, in one way or another, explored a transformation already in progress. This chapter turns instead to what lies ahead. The reflections offered here are grounded in the evidence, patterns, and analytical commitments developed throughout the earlier chapters, yet they are presented as plausible trajectories rather than firm predictions. This chapter explores four interconnected developments shaping the future of higher education. It examines artificial intelligence (AI) as it expands beyond teaching and learning into institutional strategy, governance, and administration, within the evolving regulatory frameworks of the European Union and United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO). It analyses immersive learning through virtual and augmented reality, highlighting that its impact depends less on technology itself than on infrastructure, staff readiness, and equitable access. The chapter then investigates the rise of the networked university, where platform-based collaborations and models such as micro-campuses are redefining institutional boundaries while raising new questions about power and inequality. Finally, it considers micro-credentials and digital credentialling, including blockchain-based systems, emphasising that their credibility rests on robust governance and quality assurance. Across these developments, a common theme emerges: technology does not determine educational outcomes. Its effects, whether expanding opportunity or reinforcing existing divides, depend on institutional choices, leadership, and ethical governance. The chapter concludes that the future of higher education will be shaped not primarily by technological innovation, but by the capacity of institutions and stakeholders to govern change deliberately, responsibly, and strategically.

Businesses today generate vast amounts of information through sales transactions, customer interactions, marketing campaigns, financial operations, websites and digital platforms. The challenge is no longer simply collecting this information. Organisations need professionals who can transform complex datasets into understandable reports, identify meaningful patterns and support business decisions with evidence. This is where Power BI and business analytics have become increasingly valuable. Microsoft Power BI enables professionals to connect data sources, transform information, build data models and create interactive dashboards that communicate business performance. Business analytics adds another layer by helping organisations interpret those findings and use them for planning and decision-making. The Growing Importance of Analytics Skills The Indian employment market is undergoing a significant technology-driven transformation. Recent reporting from the Times of India highlights that artificial intelligence is putting pressure on repetitive and outdated technology roles while increasing demand for professionals with skills in areas such as AI, data science, cloud computing and machine learning. This shift is making data-related capabilities increasingly relevant across industries. Organisations need professionals who can work with information, understand business requirements and communicate insights effectively. The demand is also visible in current hiring patterns. Recent job listings show Power BI being combined with skills such as SQL, DAX, Power Query, data modelling and ETL, demonstrating that modern business intelligence roles increasingly require a broader analytical toolkit rather than dashboard creation alone. For learners, this creates an opportunity to build a combination of technical and business skills through a data analytics course in Kolkata. Understanding the Role of Power BI Power BI is widely used for business intelligence and data visualisation. Its value comes from the ability to bring information from different sources into an environment where it can be transformed, analysed and presented. A typical Power BI workflow can involve importing information from spreadsheets or databases, cleaning the data, creating relationships between datasets, developing calculations and presenting the final results through interactive reports. This process teaches an important lesson in analytics: a dashboard is only as useful as the data and reasoning behind it. Learners need to understand the business purpose of each report, select appropriate metrics and ensure that the information presented is accurate and meaningful. A data analytics course in Kolkata can introduce learners to this complete workflow rather than treating Power BI as simply a chart-making application. Building a Strong Foundation Before Dashboard Development Effective Power BI work begins before the dashboard itself is created. Learners first need to understand data structures, data types, data quality and basic analytical concepts. Business datasets may contain duplicate records, missing values, inconsistent naming conventions or incorrect formats. Cleaning and preparing such information is therefore an essential stage of analytics. Power Query can help automate many data preparation and transformation activities. Learning these processes allows learners to create cleaner datasets before developing reports. This foundation is important because a visually attractive dashboard cannot compensate for unreliable underlying information. Developing Data Modelling Skills Data modelling is another important part of business intelligence. Organisations often have information stored across different tables and systems. Connecting these datasets correctly allows analysts to create more comprehensive reports. Learners can develop an understanding of relationships, dimensions, measures and structured data models. This helps them create reports that remain reliable as datasets become more complex. DAX, or Data Analysis Expressions, is also important for creating calculations and measures within Power BI. Developing familiarity with DAX can help learners move beyond basic visualisation towards more sophisticated analytical reporting. These capabilities are particularly relevant because current Power BI roles frequently mention DAX, Power Query, SQL, ETL and data modelling alongside dashboard development. Turning Dashboards into Business Intelligence The real value of Power BI appears when dashboards answer meaningful business needs. For example, a sales dashboard could show revenue by region, product category and month. A marketing dashboard could track campaign performance, customer acquisition and conversion rates. A financial report could monitor expenses, profitability and budget performance. However, the analyst's responsibility extends beyond displaying these metrics. The professional needs to identify unusual changes, recognise important trends and communicate their possible business significance. This is where business analytics becomes closely connected with Power BI. The technology helps present information, while analytical reasoning helps interpret it. Developing the Business Analytics Mindset Business analytics focuses on using data to understand organisational performance and support better decisions. An analyst may receive a requirement such as investigating declining sales. The solution could involve examining historical sales, customer segments, product categories, regional performance and marketing activity. The analyst may then use Power BI to visualise the findings and identify patterns. The final output should be more than a collection of charts. It should explain the evidence and highlight areas that deserve attention. This ability to connect technical analysis with business objectives is one of the most important capabilities learners can develop. Practical Projects and Real-World Application Projects provide an opportunity to combine multiple skills within one analytical workflow. A learner could work on a retail dataset and build a sales performance dashboard. The project might involve cleaning the data, creating a model, developing DAX measures, designing visualisations and presenting conclusions. Another project could focus on marketing analytics, where learners examine campaign performance, customer acquisition costs and conversion rates. These projects help learners understand how different components of analytics work together. They can also become part of a professional portfolio. A portfolio containing dashboards, analytical reports and case studies can demonstrate practical capability more effectively than a list of software names alone. This is particularly relevant in a skills-focused employment environment. The Economic Times reported in 2026 that Indian technology employers are increasingly emphasising practical AI capabilities and demonstrable skills, while a shortage of industry-ready talent remains a concern. Power BI, AI and the Future of Analytics Artificial intelligence is changing the way professionals interact with business data. AI-assisted tools can help automate repetitive activities, accelerate analysis and support users in exploring information. Power BI can increasingly be used alongside AI capabilities to make analytics more accessible and efficient. However, AI does not eliminate the need for analytical judgement. Professionals still need to determine whether the data is accurate, whether a pattern is meaningful and whether an automatically generated insight makes sense in the business context. Recent reporting from Moneycontrol indicates that employers are increasingly valuing workflow understanding, data skills and decision-making as enterprise AI adoption expands. Another Moneycontrol report highlighted the growing value of combining AI capabilities with existing analytical tools such as Power BI, with AI-assisted analytics emerging as an increasingly relevant workplace skill. This means future analytics professionals may benefit from learning both traditional analytical foundations and emerging AI-enabled workflows. Career Scope Across Industries Power BI and business analytics skills can be applied across a wide range of sectors. In banking and financial services, dashboards can help monitor financial performance, customer behaviour and operational metrics. In retail, analytics can support sales forecasting, inventory analysis, customer segmentation and product performance tracking. Marketing teams can use business intelligence to understand campaign results, customer acquisition and conversion rates. Healthcare organisations can apply analytics to operational performance, resource utilisation and reporting. Manufacturing and logistics businesses can use dashboards to monitor production, supply chains, inventory and delivery performance. This broad applicability creates several potential career directions, including Data Analyst, Business Intelligence Analyst, Business Analyst, Reporting Analyst, Marketing Analyst, Operations Analyst and BI Developer. documents.abstract: Soft skills are essential for university students, yet many Chinese EFL learners remain at a knowledge-telling stage, prioritizing language proficiency over interpreting acquired knowledge, while curriculum design has long centered on language hard skills with soft skills often not explicitly included as instructional objectives. This marginalization of soft skills is a persistent dilemma. Artificial intelligence, especially generative AI, is profoundly reshaping foreign language education and offering new possibilities for systematically cultivating soft skills. Nevertheless, current higher education English teaching faces two separate dilemmas: the marginalization of soft skills development, and the lack of standardization in AI use. This paper focuses on the first question of how artificial intelligence tools can systematically enhance university students’ soft skills within an English blended learning environment. This paper proposes a pedagogical design aiming to transform soft skills from implicit expectations into explicit instructional objectives.

Abstract Information campaigns are widely used to reduce household food waste, yet little is known about how consumers process the messages they receive. This study investigates whether differently framed messages trigger qualitatively different cognitive-moral responses and whether randomized message assignment changes self-reported outcomes. In a randomized two-wave experiment with Japanese consumers (Wave 1 n = 2069; Wave 2 n = 959, five-week follow-up), participants received information framed around tax burdens (Tax frame), global hunger (Hunger frame), household monetary costs (Cost frame), or a general-information control. Open-ended responses were classified into five Norm Activation Theory (NAT; [31]) stages using two independent large language model coders with researcher adjudication, supplemented by a blinded author re-coding exercise. Framing causally shifted message interpretation: the Tax and Hunger frames increased the probability of ascribing responsibility (+ 5.1 and + 5.8 percentage points), while the Cost frame uniquely elevated personal norm activation (+ 4.5 points). However, intention-to-treat estimates show no effects on self-reported preventive practices, normative orientation, or policy support. The one persistent effect is negative: five weeks later, the Tax frame reduced food waste reduction motivation (− 0.15 SD), a pattern consistent with motivational crowding-out, although the mechanism was not directly tested. Information framing changes cognitive-moral interpretation but not self-reported practices—a process-level distinction that helps explain the intention–behavior gap and informs the design of household sustainability communication.

This article develops a failure-mode framework for analyzing how advanced artificial intelligence could contribute to human extinction, irreversible civilizational collapse, or permanent human disempowerment. The central thesis is that catastrophic AI risk does not require consciousness, hostility, or an explicit intention to harm humanity. Instead, risk may arise through several distinct but interacting pathways, including autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, and competitive deployment. The severity of these pathways depends on factors such as capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, institutional safeguards, and the preservation of recovery capacity. The analysis is deliberately non-operational: it identifies causal conditions, empirically tractable intermediate quantities, and defensive research questions rather than procedures for causing harm.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Probes are the workhorse of interpretability. If a model's hidden states predict a variable, the model is said to represent it. But a probe score has no fixed meaning. An $R^2$ of 0.6 may only reflect what the input already gives away, and the same score can mean different things on different data. We propose reading every probe score against two reference points: a floor, what a declared set of simple inputs already predicts, and a ceiling, what the full input can predict. The gap between them, the headroom, is the range in which a probe can show that a model computes something beyond the simple inputs. We prove that headroom vanishes in two ways: the target stops depending on a hidden variable the model must infer, or the input stops revealing it. We test this on transformers trained for in-context meta-analysis, which must infer the hidden heterogeneity between studies to weight them correctly, and where both reference points are known. Under distribution shift, probe scores fall and prediction error rises $12$--$15\times$, yet the model recovers a similar share of the headroom, indicating that the data lost information, not the representation. We then analyze the real models. The single-cell foundation model scGPT encodes biological variability only partially. We also revisit four influential LLM probing studies, which claim that models represent geography, the state of an Othello board, truth, and the demographics of their users. Against a floor computed from the input text alone, some of these claims hold, while others are largely explained by the text itself.

While unlearning seeks to negate undesired capabilities acquired through learning, little research has examined how the way models learn shapes their subsequent unlearning. In this paper, we investigate this connection from the perspectives of memorization and generalization, the two most representative yet competing strategies that models employ during training. We first classify memorization- and generalization-heavy models using grokking in modular addition and compare their responses to unlearning, showing that the latter suffer greater retain damage, i.e., a larger performance drop on the retain set. Furthermore, we conduct a finer-grained analysis by introducing bucketed modular addition, in which the respective contributions of the two strategies can be explicitly controlled across the memorization-generalization spectrum. In this setup, we reaffirm that the same trend persists and is nearly monotonic. We further demonstrate that this relationship also holds in LLM unlearning across verbatim and factual recall settings. Finally, we provide two practical insights for developing better unlearning methods, highlighting the importance of accounting for learning dynamics in unlearning.

This chapter provides an instructor-oriented guide to teaching Chinese politics in an era shaped by geopolitical tension, pedagogical transformation and the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education. It argues that teaching China today requires more than transmitting factual knowledge; it involves helping students navigate uncertainty, contested narratives, algorithmically mediated information environments and the methodological challenges of studying politics under conditions of partial visibility. The chapter outlines how the textbook&s;s modular structure, simulations, translation literacy tools, digital literacy exercises and “How Do We Know?” epistemic framework are designed to support flexible teaching across undergraduate, postgraduate and interdisciplinary contexts, while encouraging analytical reasoning, methodological reflexivity and inclusive participation. It also examines the implications of generative AI for assessment, authorship and critical thinking, arguing for pedagogical approaches that treat AI not simply as a threat to academic integrity but as an object of critical reflection and higher-order learning. In addition, the chapter situates the textbook within broader debates on inclusive curriculum design, decolonising knowledge production and diversifying perspectives in China studies, while emphasising comparative, interdisciplinary and student-centred approaches to learning. Overall, the chapter positions the study of Chinese politics as both an intellectual and pedagogical project that equips students to think critically about governance, knowledge, technology and power in an increasingly complex global environment.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Real-world reasoning rarely reduces to static question answering: agents must actively gather information from tools and sensors that are often noisy and unreliable. Yet most existing active reasoning benchmarks assume that environmental feedback is trustworthy, or introduce noise without exposing an explicit, calibrated uncertainty signal, leaving open how LLMs should reason when the evidence itself is uncertain. We introduce VisualNoiseQA, a novel benchmark for active reasoning under noisy visual feedback. A text-only LLM must solve VQA problems by iteratively querying a fixed, off-the-shelf VLM treated as a stochastic visual sensor. For each query, we draw multiple samples and expose an empirical uncertainty signal via self-consistency, enabling the reasoner to probe from different angles and decide what to ask next and when to stop. Our construction is automatic and scalable: starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, we retain only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable. We evaluate multiple LLM reasoners on 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. VisualNoiseQA thus provides a controlled playground to study how different LLMs exploit uncertainty signals for robust reasoning.

Accurate voxel-level segmentation of pulmonary nodules on chest CT is needed for diameter and volume measurement, growth tracking, and quantitative assessment in lung cancer screening. The task remains difficult: nodules vary in attenuation, size, and contact with vessels or pleura, and clinically relevant morphology often lies in a thin, ambiguous margin. Existing systems commonly trade contour fidelity for speed—large prompt-driven foundation models can be accurate but slow, whereas compact CNN or SSM decoders are efficient yet tend to smooth spiculated and ground-glass borders. We propose HSV-Net (Hybrid State-space–Vision Network), a dual-stream 3D network that is prompt-free after nodule localization: an SSM3D stream provides whole-patch context with linear-complexity state-space blocks, and an OrthoLoRA stream adapts frozen DINOv2 features on axial, coronal, and sagittal slices. A Hybrid Gated Mixer (HGM) fuses the two streams before FPN decoding, and Progressive Contour Learning (PCL) supervises overlap, signed-distance-field geometry, and uncertainty-weighted contour refinement. On a 10-patient QIN Lung CT/QIN-LungCT-Seg development subset ( n = 12 tumors; nested patient-level 5-fold CV), HSV-Net obtained the highest mean Dice (90.1% ± 1.0%; 95% CI [88.9, 91.3]) and Boundary F1 (86.3% ± 1.3%) among the compared methods on 128 × 128 × 64 patches, with a latency of 58 ms. A standard full-volume nnU-Net v2 baseline reached 88.6% ± 1.0% Dice on the same QIN folds, still below HSV-Net. On an independent LIDC-IDRI benchmark with expert volumetric consensus masks (186 patients/294 nodules; patient-level 5-fold CV within LIDC, not QIN→LIDC transfer), HSV-Net achieved 87.8% ± 1.1% Dice and 83.6% ± 1.3% Boundary F1, outperforming full-volume nnU-Net (87.1% ± 1.0% Dice). LUNA16 was retained only as a proxy size/localization check with diameter-matched spherical references, not as contour external validation.
